problem: Prior work treats guiding and object retrieval as separate systems, and LLM-based multi-robot planners often equate a valid-looking plan with task success. Nothing verifies whether heterogeneous robots can exploit concurrency while symbolic progress matches physically verified completion.
motivation: Assistive robot dogs for blind users should both guide the user to a seat and fetch and deliver an object. That requires capability-aware role assignment, dependency handling, and completion measured from robot and object state. The paper separates plan validity, execution progress and mission completion to avoid false success and misleading speedups from early failures.
key_idea: An LLM fills a schedule-conditioned four-action schema. A deterministic validator and compiler enforce capabilities and dependencies, and state-based terminal checks decide success for a guider-plus-fetcher team executing sequentially or in parallel.
insight: Plan validity did not predict mission success: all 180 online plans validated, yet 37 of 180 schedule runs failed in manipulation. The paired makespan gain (41.3%) mixes role assignment, overlap and scene geometry. In Home and Supermarket total distance rose while time fell, which points to overlap. In Hospital total distance also fell (68.25 to 40.60 m), which points to role reassignment. Because the LLM output always matched the script, the plan-provenance comparison only tests normalized-plan agreement.
method: Schedule-conditioned plan instantiation: a local Qwen3.5-4B receives the robots, skills, registered targets and a preselected schedule, and outputs JSON with four action records (step, robot, skill, target, params).

Deterministic validation: parses the JSON, normalizes aliases, resolves targets against the scene registry, and checks action inventory, capabilities and schedule structure. The mutation test accepts 2 controls and rejects 32/32 mutants.
Dependency compiler: builds nominal levels from step indices (parallel: 3 levels of 2/1/1 actions; sequential: 4 single-action levels) with no global barriers.
Shared-clock executor: branch-local state machines (pending/running/succeeded/failed) advance under one 200 Hz simulation clock, and failures propagate through dependencies.

Robot skills: the Go2 guider uses a PPO recurrent lidar policy with kinematic waypoint transport. The B2+Z1 fetcher uses an ALORE-derived locomotion policy with IK arm staging, and its base is transported along registered routes.

State-based completion checks: bilateral contact, lift ≥30 mm, a 1 s retention hold (≥20 mm rise, tilt ≤17°, grasp-reference distance ≤0.25 m), then delivery. Operational success is the conjunction of visit, pickup, grasp, lift, retain and delivery.
Paired evaluation design: 3 GRScenes × 30 seeds × {sequential, parallel} × {scripted, online} = 360 runs, with makespan compared only over common successes.

numbers_note: Custom benchmark only, no standard navigation benchmark. Per-scene results are in Table 2 and not duplicated as entries.
results: Sequential and parallel schedules reach 72/90 and 71/90 operational success. Over 56 common successes the parallel schedule cuts mean makespan from 164.78 to 96.79 s (41.3%, bootstrap CI [54.05, 82.04] s). All 180 online Qwen3.5 plans validated on the first request and matched the scripted plans, and the validator rejected 32/32 mutants.
limitations: Language evidence is limited to four paraphrase templates and a fixed schema, with the schedule given to the prompt. The LLM never chooses the schedule, so no open-ended planning or replanning is tested.

Simulation-only, with kinematic route transport, disabled collision response, one lightweight object (5 g) and checks that stop before assisted transport. Guidance is proxied by destination arrival with no human modeled.
Manipulation causes all failures, and the speedup is a system-level mix of role assignment, overlap and scene geometry rather than an isolated concurrency effect.
